intro.en: How a child with suspected heart disease is examined, from pulses and pressures to murmurs, diagnosis and blueness.

title.en: History, pulses and pressures in suspected heart disease

items.summary: The bedside numbers recorded first: pulse, breathing rate, pressures in all limbs, neck veins and refill time, plus two pressure sums.

blocks.title: Bedside numbers
bullets: Record pulse rate, breathing rate, blood pressure, neck vein height and refill time in every cardiac child.
Take the pressure in both arms and both legs when heart disease is suspected.
Take a standing pressure as well to catch a drop on standing.

blocks.title: Pressure sums
bullets: Pulse pressure is the top figure minus the bottom figure; it runs wide with a leaky aortic valve and narrow with a tight one.
Average pressure is the bottom figure plus one third of the pulse pressure.
For a newborn the book links the expected figure to the weeks of pregnancy plus 10.

viva.q: Why take pressure in all four limbs?
viva.a: A gap between arm and leg readings points to narrowing of the aorta.

viva.q: What do wide and narrow pulse pressures suggest?
viva.a: A wide gap suggests a leaky aortic valve and a narrow gap a tight one.

viva.q: How is average pressure worked out?
viva.a: Bottom figure plus one third of the gap between top and bottom figures.

unsure: The book's newborn formula, weeks of pregnancy plus 10, does not state which pressure it estimates, so it needs checking against the manual.

title.en: Grading effort tolerance and Nada criteria

items.summary: Two bedside grading sets: four classes for breathlessness on effort and the major-minor yardstick that suggests heart disease.

head: Class
Meaning
rows: No symptoms with usual play and activity
Symptoms with usual activity such as walking to school
Symptoms with daily care such as bathing or using the toilet

blocks.title: When heart disease is called
blocks.text: The book calls heart disease present when any one major sign or any two minor signs are found.

groups.label: Major signs
bullets: Loud systolic murmur of grade 3 or more
Any diastolic murmur
Blue lips and tongue
Frank pump failure

groups.label: Minor signs
bullets: Soft systolic murmur below grade 3
Odd second heart sound
Odd heart tracing
Odd chest film
Odd blood pressure reading

viva.q: What separates class 2 from class 3?
viva.a: Class 2 limits usual activity like school walks, class 3 limits daily care like bathing.

viva.q: How many Nada signs call heart disease?
viva.a: Any one major sign or any two minor signs together.

viva.q: Give one major and one minor murmur sign.
viva.a: A systolic murmur of grade 3 or more is major, below grade 3 is minor.

title.en: Inspection of the front of the chest

items.summary: Looking at the shape of the chest wall, the strongest beat, extra throbs, skin marks and the spine before laying hands on.

blocks.title: What to look for
bullets: Note whether the chest wall looks flat or bulges forward over the heart.
Find where the strongest beat shows, normally the fourth rib gap inside the nipple line.
Look for extra throbs at the pit of the neck, the second left gap and the pit of the stomach.
Look for scars, discharging openings and full surface veins.
Check the backbone runs straight without a hunch or a sideways bend.

viva.q: What does a forward bulge of the chest wall suggest?
viva.a: Long standing enlargement of the heart pushing the soft chest out.

viva.q: Which extra throbs do you look for?
viva.a: Throbs at the neck pit, the second left gap and the pit of the stomach.

title.en: Feeling the heartbeat, thrills and pulses

items.summary: Confirming the strongest beat and its feel, hunting for lifts, hums and thrills, then comparing the limb pulses on both sides.

blocks.title: Heart and neck
bullets: Confirm the strongest beat in the fourth rib gap inside the nipple line and note if it feels confined or spread.
Note the feel of the beat and any palpable first sound, lung valve shut or throb at the pit of the stomach.
Feel for a right sided lift beside the breastbone with the palm edge.
Feel for a humming thrill at the base of the neck.
Feel the neck artery for a bounding throb or a buzzing thrill.

blocks.title: Limb arteries
bullets: Feel the arm, wrist, groin and foot pulses on both sides together.
Note any delay, weakness or absence between upper and lower limbs.

viva.q: What does a right sided lift mean?
viva.a: It points to an enlarged right pumping chamber straining against pressure.

viva.q: Which pulses must be felt together?
viva.a: Arm, wrist, groin and foot pulses on both sides, to catch aortic narrowing.

viva.q: What is a thrill?
viva.a: A buzzing vibration felt on the chest or artery over a loud murmur.

title.en: Percussion of the heart and liver

items.summary: Tapping out the heart edges and the liver span, a short step that backs up what inspection and feeling found.

blocks.title: Borders to mark
bullets: Match the left heart edge to the strongest beat.
Match the right heart edge to the side edge of the breastbone.
Mark the top of the liver at the right fifth rib gap and note its span in centimetres.
Check for a dull patch in the right second rib gap.

viva.q: Where is the right heart edge in a child?
viva.a: At the side edge of the breastbone on gentle tapping.

viva.q: Why mark the liver span in a cardiac child?
viva.a: A tender enlarged liver is an early sign of pump failure backing up.

title.en: Listening to the four valve areas

items.summary: A fixed order round the mitral, tricuspid, aortic and pulmonary spots, then the extra sounds and the belly, lung and eye checks.

groups.label: Tip area for the mitral valve
bullets: Listen at the strongest beat for the first and second sounds and any murmur.

groups.label: Lower breastbone for the tricuspid valve
bullets: Listen at the lower left end of the breastbone for both sounds and any murmur.

groups.label: Right second gap for the aortic valve
bullets: Listen right of the breastbone in the second rib gap for both sounds and any murmur.

groups.label: Left second gap for the pulmonary valve
bullets: Listen left of the breastbone in the second rib gap, noting a loud lung component.

blocks.title: Extra listening and checks
bullets: Listen for a snapping sound, an ejection click and a friction rub.
Carry the stethoscope to the neck arteries and out toward the armpit.
Look for signs of a leaky aortic valve, valve infection and pump failure.
Feel the belly for an enlarged liver and free fluid.
Listen at the lung bases for crackles and inspect the back of the eye.

viva.q: Where do you listen for the aortic valve?
viva.a: Right of the breastbone in the second rib gap, with the child sitting forward.

viva.q: Why listen over the neck arteries and armpit?
viva.a: Murmurs often spread there, which helps name the valve at fault.

viva.q: Which bedside checks complete the cardiac look?
viva.a: Belly for liver and fluid, lung bases for crackles and the eye back wall.

items.summary: The features to state for every murmur, the six loudness grades, and two positioning tricks that bring soft murmurs out.

blocks.title: Features of every murmur
bullets: State the site where it sounds loudest.
State its timing in systole or diastole.
State its loudness grade from 1 to 6.
State where it spreads.
State its tone and pitch.
State whether bell or diaphragm shows it best.
State how it shifts with breath, posture and exercise.

blocks.title: Memory hook
blocks.text: The book offers PQRST for pitch, quality, spread, site and thrill felt on the chest.

head: Grade
Meaning
rows: Very faint, heard only with full attention
Faint but picked up easily on listening
Heard even with one edge of the chestpiece lifted
Heard even with the chestpiece fully off the wall

blocks.title: Positioning tricks
bullets: Roll the child to the left side and rest the bell lightly at the tip to catch mitral narrowing.
Sit the child up leaning forward and use the diaphragm from the right second gap down the left edge for a leaky aortic valve.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A low rumbling mid diastolic murmur of grade 2, loudest at the tip on breathing out in left side lying with the bell, without spread, with a late accentuation.

viva.q: What seven points describe any murmur?
viva.a: Site, timing, grade, spread, tone, best chestpiece and change with breath or posture.

viva.q: How do you bring out mitral narrowing?
viva.a: Roll the child left, rest the bell lightly at the tip and listen on breathing out.

viva.q: How do you bring out a leaky aortic valve?
viva.a: Sit the child forward and use the diaphragm down the left sternal edge.

unsure: The book's PQRST expansion differs from the standard pain mnemonic, so it was kept as printed for review.

items.summary: The six lines examiners expect before the final sentence: disease type, valve, lung pressures, infection, failure and rhythm.

blocks.title: Six lines
bullets: Name the disease family: pink or blue birth defect of the heart, or rheumatic valve disease.
Name the valve at fault: leaking or narrowed mitral or aortic valve.
State whether lung pressures look high.
State whether valve infection looks present.
State whether pump failure looks present.
State the rhythm, usually normal sinus rhythm.

blocks.title: Worked line
blocks.text: Rheumatic valve disease with a tight mitral valve and high lung pressures, no sign of valve infection, no failure, in normal rhythm.

viva.q: What six points frame the diagnosis?
viva.a: Disease type, valve, lung pressures, infection, failure and rhythm.

viva.q: Why name lung pressures separately?
viva.a: High lung pressures change treatment and follow up whatever the valve lesion.

title.en: Valve infection signs and two kinds of blueness

items.summary: Bedside clues of infected valves, and how central blueness of tongue and lips differs from cold blue fingers and toes.

blocks.title: Clues of valve infection
bullets: Look for fever, paleness and curved nails in a child with a known murmur.
Look for painless palm spots, tender finger nodes and nail streak bleeds.
Look for pale centred spots at the back of the eye.
Feel for a big spleen and ask about new weakness or fits.

head: Feature
Central
Cold peripheral
rows: Lips, tongue tip, nose tip, ears, mouth lining, nails
No change in heart causes, falls in lung causes

viva.q: Name three skin or nail clues of valve infection.
viva.a: Painless palm spots, tender finger nodes and streak bleeds under the nails.

viva.q: How does warming separate the two bluenesses?
viva.a: Cold blue tips fade on warming while central blueness stays put.

viva.q: How does oxygen help tell heart from lung causes?
viva.a: Heart cause blueness persists on oxygen while lung cause blueness falls.

unsure: The book's last row on oxygen response was hard to align after page extraction, so the heart cause versus lung cause wording should be checked.
